children.name: Local and Air-Gapped Model Deployment
children.blurb: Local and air-gapped model deployment covers running language models, document review classifiers, and other AI systems entirely within a law firm's or legal department's own infrastructure, with no connection to external cloud services.

children.name: Secure Storage and Networking for Legal Data
children.blurb: Secure storage and networking for legal data covers the systems and practices that protect client files, case strategy, privileged communications, contracts, and e-discovery materials from unauthorized access, loss, or alteration.

children.name: Timekeeping and Billing Narratives
children.blurb: AI-assisted timekeeping and billing narratives cover the creation, review, and standardization of time entries and invoice descriptions in legal practice.

children.name: Firm Knowledge Management
children.blurb: Firm knowledge management in this context means the systems and practices a law firm uses to capture, organize, retrieve, and reuse its internal work product, including matter files, precedent clauses, research memoranda, playbooks, client preferences, and training materials.

children.name: Client Intake and Triage
children.blurb: Client intake and triage covers the initial capture, conflict checking, matter classification, urgency assessment, and routing of new legal work requests.

sections.body: Legal operations, infrastructure and security is the part of AI in law that deals with how a firm runs its own systems, protects client data and turns legal work into a billable record. In practice, AI is being used to run local or air-gapped models on firm hardware, to search and summarize internal documents, to draft time entries and billing narratives, to route new matters at intake and to classify documents for privilege or relevance. The work is not mainly about arguing motions in court. It is about retrieval, redaction, access control, logging, encryption, backup and the unglamorous plumbing that lets lawyers use a model without sending confidential material to an outside service. Firms are also using AI to answer routine client questions, to extract dates and parties from intake forms and to suggest matter codes before a human reviews the file.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field has real solved pieces, including encrypted storage, role-based access, private networking, local inference for some models and automated first drafts of billing narratives. What is not solved is trust at the edges, because a model can still summarize incorrectly, miss a privilege flag, leak context through a prompt or produce a billing line that a client disputes. Air-gapped deployment reduces some network risk but often means smaller or older models, more maintenance and slower updates, so it is a trade-off rather than a clean win. The site tracks 215 compliance and regulation pages and 6940 state AI bills, which shows how much of this work is about keeping systems inside shifting rules. The site also tracks 146 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, so data handling and output use remain contested. Honest limits include weak evaluation for legal tasks, unclear liability when an intake triage tool misroutes a matter and the difficulty of auditing a model that changes with each update.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section fit together as a stack, with deployment and security as the base and the operational workflows as the layers above. Local and Air-Gapped Model Deployment is for a reader who needs to know what it takes to run a model on firm-controlled hardware, including hardware limits, model choice and update paths. Secure Storage and Networking for Legal Data covers the controls around that deployment, such as encryption, segmentation, access logs and safe connections between offices, clouds and remote workers. Client Intake and Triage is the front door, where a reader can see how AI sorts new matters, extracts facts and flags urgency before a lawyer takes over. Firm Knowledge Management is the internal library, where a reader can learn how AI searches precedent, memos and work product without losing the source trail. Timekeeping and Billing Narratives is the back office, where a reader can see how AI turns calendar entries, emails and task logs into draft bills that a human still has to review.
